claim: A side cart can lift AOV with a multi-step progress bar (free shipping, then a free gift), one-click low-price cross-sells and an in-cart switch to subscribe-and-save.
body: In the teardown the side cart, not the product page, carries several AOV levers. Mechanism: the shopper has already decided, so small adds priced well below the main item feel trivial, and a visible next threshold turns spending more into progress toward a reward. Elements to copy: 1) A progress bar with more than one unlock: first free shipping, then a free gift, so the shopper who already qualified for shipping still has a reason to add. 2) A one-click 'add to your order' row of cross-sells priced around 9 to 24 against a main bundle, with no product page visit needed. 3) When a one-time item is added, offer an in-cart upgrade to subscribe and save (the source cites a Shopify app for this). 4) A sticky checkout button that stays visible while scrolling, with the savings and correct total shown. 5) On Shopify Plus, repeat reviews and perks (easy returns, customer count) in checkout with the same button colour and styling. The source also shows a 'reserving your order for X minutes due to high demand' timer. No conversion or AOV lift figures are given, so measure the cross-sell attach rate and AOV change yourself before and after.
conditions: Shopify stores with a side (drawer) cart, a catalogue of low-priced add-ons and a free-shipping threshold; checkout customisation only on Shopify Plus.
fails_when: There are no genuinely relevant low-price add-ons, so cross-sells add clutter; or the reservation timer is false, which risks consumer-protection complaints about fake urgency (for example UK CMA or EU UCPD rules) and erodes trust with repeat buyers.

claim: Advertorial benchmarks: 30-40% click through to the next page, 70-80% from a second pre-sell page onward, and about 15% conversion on the final checkout page.
body: The practitioner's funnel targets: from the first advertorial page, about 30% of visitors should click through, ideally 40%; from a second pre-sell page, 70 to 80% should continue; the final checkout page (he uses a funnel-builder checkout) should convert around 15%. In the first 48 hours, judge only engagement: CPM, ad CTR, scroll depth and page-to-page click-through. Then work down the funnel step by step. Page structure that the benchmarks assume: hook or shocking discovery; who this is for; cost of doing nothing; why the problem happens; why each alternative fails; three kinds of proof (mechanism that makes logical sense, reviews ideally from repeat buyers, and a visual demonstration); offer reveal, often with price held back until the second page; objections on risk, price, time and safety; guarantee; then a soft, medium or hard CTA. Place CTAs about four times: after the hook, after the mechanism, after proof, and after objections and guarantee (or use a sticky button). Assets to gather first: 10 to 20 review quotes, five objections, a three-sentence mechanism. Test order: format first, then headline, then position of the first proof block. CTA style rarely matters and needs thousands of daily visitors to read.
conditions: Multi-step advertorial funnels on paid social traffic; benchmarks are one practitioner's, from health and beauty style offers.
fails_when: Traffic is too low to read page-to-page rates (CTA style tests need thousands of visitors a day); the funnel is a single page to a standard Shopify PDP, where checkout conversion of 15% is not comparable; benchmarks have no stated sample.

claim: Choose the advertorial format by the buying obstacle: low trust, story; needs permission, expert; scepticism or too many options, buyer's guide; 'will it work for me', case study.
body: The source lists six advertorial formats and says to choose by the obstacle that stops the sale, not by taste. Story format (a person's failed attempts, the discovery, the change) suits cold traffic with emotional or identity problems and low trust; put proof early. Authority or expert format (dermatologist, vet, doctor describing 'what I see in patients') suits buyers who need permission to act, common in health, beauty, pain and pets; use real, verifiable experts. Buyer's guide or 'top 5' comparison suits sceptical, seen-it-all buyers or buyers overwhelmed by options; it names the alternatives they are weighing and explains why each falls short, so the click arrives pre-sold, and it also works on retargeting. Industry-exposé format (small lab versus a huge industry) taps distrust of big brands. Case study format walks through one problem, each standard solution that failed, then the product, and answers 'will this work for someone like me' (age, skin type, ethnicity). Listicle 'reasons why' handles several objections at once. To find the obstacle, read ad comments, support emails and forums for repeated doubts. Then test formats against each other (story versus guide) before testing anything smaller.
conditions: Pre-sell pages for cold paid traffic in categories with trust or claim barriers.
fails_when: Comparison pages make false or unverifiable claims about named competitors (legal risk), experts are fabricated, or the format does not match the real objection found in research; on low-trust categories, an obviously fake 'news' look can lower trust.

claim: Send cold traffic to an advertorial instead of the product page when the product needs about three minutes of explanation; simple, understood products go straight to the PDP.
body: A product page assumes the visitor already wants the item and only needs the price. For many cold visitors that is false: they see '$50' before they understand why the product is worth it, and leave. An advertorial (a native, article-style pre-sell page) builds the desire first. The practitioner's rule of thumb: if the product's value takes roughly three minutes to explain, it needs an advertorial; a bottle of water, a mouse pad or a plain t-shirt does not. Signals that you need one: the market is sceptical, the claims need explaining, the product works through a new or unfamiliar mechanism, or the category is crowded with look-alike offers (common in health, beauty, pain relief, pets, gadgets and weight loss). Match the page to awareness: product-aware and most-aware visitors (retargeting, branded search, existing customers) can go straight to the PDP with an offer; unaware and problem-aware visitors need the story, the cause of the problem and the mechanism before they see a price. The practitioner claims the advertorial route is what lets unaware and problem-aware campaigns scale to very high daily spend. Practical step: before building, write down the awareness level of the traffic source and the one objection that most often stops purchase, then choose the page type.
conditions: Cold prospecting traffic for products with a mechanism, claim or category that needs explaining; DTC brands on paid social.
fails_when: The product is simple, impulse-priced or already understood, or the traffic is warm/product-aware, where an extra page adds friction; health and weight-loss claims in advertorials can breach ad platform and consumer-protection rules if not substantiated.

claim: Ask buyers what almost stopped them, then place 3 to 4 hand-picked reviews answering those exact objections beside the bundle selector and add-to-cart button.
body: Generic proof (press logos, a wall of stars) is everywhere, so it does little. The agency's method: 1) survey recent buyers and run user tests asking 'what almost stopped you buying today?' and 'what made you buy?'; 2) list the top objections; 3) pick 3 to 4 reviews that answer those objections in the customer's words; 4) place them at the point of action, next to the bundle choice and add-to-cart button, or above the fold. Example: for a respirator brand, research showed the main fears were 'will this actually protect me' and 'will it fog up', so the chosen review mentioned protection for eyes and lungs, sparks, dust and no fogging. If price is the main objection, choose reviews about value for money. If you have only about 30 reviews, showing a review count can hurt, so feature a few strong, relevant quotes instead. A beauty brand cited does the same with press quotes about specific results rather than outlet logos. No lift numbers are given for this tactic.
conditions: Product pages where buyers have known, nameable objections (efficacy, fit, comfort, price); works with small review counts.
fails_when: No customer research to identify objections, so the reviews are guesses; categories where shoppers expect to see full review counts and distributions (marketplaces).

claim: Cutting bundle choices from five (1, 2, 3, 5, 10-pack) to three (1, 3, 5) lifted conversion 53% and average order value 13.5% for a drinks brand.
body: An agency's test for Wildman Drinking. Session recordings showed shoppers at the bundle selector either picking the 1 or 2-pack or leaving the site. The hypothesis was choice overload: too many close options make comparison hard, so people default to the cheapest or defer. Reducing to three options (1, 3 and 5-pack) raised conversion rate 53% and average order value 13.5% at the same time, because the remaining tiers were spaced far enough apart to make the step up obvious. How to apply: 1) watch recordings and click maps of your bundle or variant selector; 2) list each option's share of orders; 3) drop tiers with negligible take or that sit too close to a neighbour; 4) keep a single unit, a typical-use multiple and a stock-up option; 5) A/B test, reading conversion and AOV separately. Caveat: the source gives no sample size, test length or traffic level, so treat the size of the lift as a hypothesis to test, not a benchmark.
conditions: Consumables or multi-pack products sold through a quantity selector on the product page; enough traffic to A/B test.
fails_when: Products where buyers genuinely need many quantity or size options (B2B, varied usage); single high-ticket items; very low-traffic stores that cannot validate the change.
numbers: 5 options to 3: conversion +53%, AOV +13.5% (no sample size given)

claim: Keep main navigation under 7 items and remove product-page elements that get under 1% of clicks; one brand saw monthly orders rise 60% after this and other changes.
body: The agency treats clutter as a conversion cost. Navigation: they see diminishing returns above seven top-level items, so they cut menu items that click maps show nobody uses. Product pages: in one audit (Sumach), most side elements on the product page drew under 1% of clicks, several at 0 to 0.21%. Removing that clutter, combined with other changes, coincided with a 60% increase in monthly online orders. Because several changes shipped together, the 60% cannot be credited to removal alone. How to apply: 1) install a click-map tool and collect at least a few thousand sessions per template; 2) rank every link and module on the page by share of clicks; 3) remove or collapse anything below about 1% that is not legally required or a trust element people read without clicking (shipping and returns notes); 4) cut navigation to the categories that carry most clicks and revenue; 5) ship one change at a time if you want to know what worked. Beware that low clicks does not mean low value for reassurance content.
conditions: Stores with cluttered menus or product pages and enough traffic for reliable click maps.
fails_when: Large catalogues where shoppers navigate deep category trees; reassurance content (returns, sizing) that matters without being clicked; changes bundled so the cause is unknown.

elements with under 1% of clicks (0-0.92% observed)
monthly orders +60% after several combined changes

claim: Putting bundle savings as dollars in the option title ('3 pack, save $10') instead of a percentage in small text raised conversion 25% and revenue per visitor 28.6%.
body: Same agency, same drinks brand. The original bundle selector showed '10% savings' and '20% savings' in body text under each option. The variant moved the saving into the option headline and stated it in dollars: '3 pack, save $10' and '5 pack, save $20'. Reported result: conversion rate up 25% and revenue per user up 28.57%. The principle is 'do not make the shopper do maths': a dollar figure next to the choice is read at a glance, while a percentage in small print requires calculation and is often skipped. How to apply: 1) state the saving in currency when the dollar amount is meaningful (percentages can read bigger on cheap items, so test both); 2) put it in the line people actually read, the option title; 3) keep the arithmetic honest against the single-unit price; 4) A/B test and read conversion and revenue per visitor, not conversion alone. No sample size or duration was reported, so the size of the lift is unverified.
conditions: Multi-pack or bundle selectors where the saving per tier is a few dollars or more.
fails_when: Very low-priced items where a percentage looks larger than the dollar figure; savings computed against an inflated reference price, which can be misleading.

revenue per user +28.57%

claim: Replace pop-ups that fire in the first 3 to 5 seconds with exit-intent, post-add-to-cart or scroll-depth triggers; the agency reports conversion gains up to 125% from timing alone.
body: The argument: a pop-up in the first seconds interrupts visitors who do not yet know what the brand sells, adding friction and exits. Fewer people see a well-timed pop-up, but those who do are engaged, so conversions rise; the agency says it has seen up to 125% increases just by changing timing (no sample given). Three triggers they use: 1) exit intent, for first-time visitors about to leave, offering a first-order discount for an email address so they can be re-marketed; 2) right after add to cart, aimed at hesitant, price-sensitive shoppers, offering a small incentive to finish; 3) scroll depth, set at the point where recordings or scroll maps show interest drops (for example if half of readers abandon midway through the product description), offering help or a discount there. How to apply: check scroll and exit data first, set the trigger at the measured drop-off point, and compare email capture rate and store conversion before and after. Note the discount-on-add-to-cart trigger can train shoppers to wait for it.
conditions: Stores using email-capture or discount pop-ups with enough traffic to measure drop-off points; mostly first-time visitors.
fails_when: Mobile layouts where exit intent cannot fire reliably; returning customers who learn to trigger discounts; brands avoiding discounting altogether.

claim: Set headlines 3 to 4 times the body text size: with 16px desktop body copy, a 48 to 57px headline.
body: The agency's most common audit finding on visual hierarchy is a headline barely larger than the body text, so the value proposition, which many visitors read alone, carries no visual weight. Their rule of thumb: make the headline 3 to 4 times the body size; with the usual 16px desktop body text that means roughly 48 to 57px. Hierarchy also comes from colour and placement: a contrasting colour reserved for the add-to-cart button and announcement bar, a different tone for headline versus body, and nothing else competing for that accent colour. A quick test: blur a screenshot of the page; the primary call to action should still be the obvious thing to click. In their before-and-after example the 'before' mobile page had an oversized logo and announcement bar and a button that did not stand out; the 'after' used a large headline, lighter body, and an orange button, so the eye moved top to bottom. How to apply: audit font sizes in the theme settings for desktop and mobile separately, since mobile scales differ, and keep one accent colour for actions.
conditions: Hero and product page sections on desktop; scale proportionally on mobile, where 3-4x can be too large for long headlines.
fails_when: Long headlines on narrow mobile screens, where 48px wraps into many lines and pushes the CTA below the fold; brands with editorial typography where size contrast is carried another way.

claim: Advertorial CTAs convert better as soft steps: 'Check availability' with no price, a line above the button telling readers to click, and a second CTA after an author note.
body: The copywriter's view is that an advertorial must not switch into a hard sell at the end, because the reader came for a story. So the product is handed over softly. A character in the story asks where to get it (his example: the doctor was so impressed he asked where to buy it). The button says 'Check availability' rather than 'Buy now, $50 off', and the price is not named on the advertorial; price and offer live on the product page. Directly above the button, one line tells the reader to click the button below to check availability, which removes doubt about the next step. Below the first CTA, add a short, personal note about the author (for example, that they love tennis), then a second CTA, because people buy from people. On Taboola or other native traffic, use more CTAs and a shorter article. How to apply: audit your current advertorial's last screen against these four points. No conversion data is given; these are rules from his own practice.
conditions: Story advertorials sending cold traffic to a separate product or offer page; health, wellness and problem-solution products.
fails_when: The advertorial is the only page before checkout so price must be shown; offer-led promotions (sales events) where the discount is the hook; ad platforms or categories whose policies restrict implied scarcity or testimonial-style claims.

claim: Edit an advertorial by marking every sentence where the story stops and the pitch starts; each marked sentence is a likely exit point, so rewrite it inside the narrative.
body: The most common failure this copywriter sees is an advertorial that opens with 100 to 200 words of story and then turns into ordinary sales copy once the product appears. Readers accept a story but resist being sold to, so the switch is where they close the tab. His editing method: read the draft back and highlight every sentence where narration ends and selling begins, then rewrite each one so the product arrives through the plot. Ways to do that: tell it from a third person such as a doctor seeing a patient; have the main character try the product despite advice against it; let the result be shown by the character's life (playing tennis again) rather than claimed. Write the after state first, then work backwards and spend most of the words on the before state so the contrast is strong. Give the product's mechanism a short name the reader could repeat at a party. Single-practitioner advice with no test numbers; mainly drawn from knee-pain and supplement offers.
conditions: Long-form advertorials for problem-solution products sold to cold traffic, especially health and wellness.
fails_when: Readers want specs and comparison (technical or high-consideration products) rather than a story; regulated health claims where a dramatised doctor narrative or invented patient would breach ad or consumer-protection rules; brands whose voice cannot carry a fictional first-person story.
numbers: typical failing draft: 100 to 200 words of story before the pitch takes over

claim: On an advertorial, show a sticky buy button only after the reader scrolls past the paragraph that introduces the product, never during the problem section.
body: Advertorials (pre-landers) work by keeping the reader inside a story about a problem they recognise, then introducing the product as the thing that resolved it. A health and wellness copywriter who says he has written hundreds of them argues that a sticky 'Check availability' or buy button that appears early, or at a fixed 50% scroll depth, breaks this. It tells a reader who is still problem-aware that this is a sales page before the product has been introduced, which is the point where people leave. How to apply: set the sticky bar to trigger on an element, not a percentage. Place an invisible anchor just after the product-introduction paragraph and only show the sticky CTA once that anchor has scrolled out of view. Keep in-line CTAs below that point too. Check on mobile, where sticky bars take a larger share of the screen. This is a practitioner rule with no test data in the source; confirm it with your own split test of trigger position if traffic allows.
conditions: Story-format advertorials or listicles sent cold traffic from Meta or native ads, where readers arrive problem-aware but not product-aware.
fails_when: The page is a product page or a short pre-lander for warm or retargeted traffic that already knows the product; very short native advertorials where the product appears in the first screen.

claim: On a lead-gen page, a top button scrolling to a form on the same page beat sending visitors to a separate opt-in page, +220% in one test.
body: The presenter's agency ran an A/B test on a B2B lead-generation page where the original flow sent visitors from the landing page to a separate opt-in page. The variant placed a 'learn more' button at the top of the page that scrolled the visitor down to the contact form embedded on the same page. Conversions rose 220% in the test. Session recordings explained why: visitors read the value proposition, image and stats, clicked within about 6 to 7 seconds, landed on the form with the page's arguments still in view, and filled it straight away, instead of facing a new page that made them re-decide. Supporting rules from the same source: repeat the call to action down the page so a visitor can convert at whichever section persuades them; keep forms to four fields or fewer, combine first and last name into one field; and put a short line beside the form saying what happens next. How to apply: if your conversion step lives on another URL, test an in-page anchor to an embedded form or a sticky button that scrolls there. Treat the 220% as one agency-reported test with no sample size, not an expected lift.

claim: Write sponsored editorial and advertorial-style emails as roughly 70 percent genuinely useful or entertaining content and at most 30 percent pitch.
body: Readers skim past anything that looks like an ad but read, finish and share content that helps or entertains them, and they lend that content the trust they give the host publication or sender. The practitioner's working ratio is about 70 percent real value (a story, a how-to, product use tips, a funny listicle) and no more than 30 percent promotion. At AppSumo, daily deal emails to around 750,000 subscribers were written this way: most of the email explained the product's benefits and how to use it, and the deal itself took under 30 percent of the space, which he reports drove more engagement, full reads and purchases and fewer unsubscribes than straight 'buy this' sends. The older benchmark he cites is Ogilvy's reference-guide ads (a stain-removal guide, a beer and oyster pairing guide) that readers tore out and kept. How to apply: draft the useful piece first so it would stand alone, then weave in the product as the natural tool and close with the offer. No controlled test or sample is given; treat the ratio as a starting heuristic.
conditions: Sponsored placements on publishers, native ads and frequent promotional email sends to an engaged list where unsubscribes are the main cost of over-pitching.
fails_when: Direct-response pre-sell advertorials for cold paid traffic, where the page is built to move a reader to a product page and a longer, more explicit pitch is normal; bottom-of-funnel traffic already searching for the product, where value padding delays the sale.

claim: Test the headline first and the hero image second; the agency attributes its largest lifts, up to 130 percent, to above-the-fold changes because many visitors never scroll.
body: The top of the page is the only part every visitor sees, and the agency cites a figure (unsourced) that about 60 percent never scroll past it, so changes there touch the most traffic. Their testing order is: first make sure the headline says who you are, what you do and what the buyer gets, readable in five seconds; then test variations of that benefit; then test the image under the headline so it shows the value proposition rather than decorating it. Reported results across B2B and ecommerce clients: headline tests up to 60 to 80 percent conversion lift, above-the-fold tests overall up to 130 percent, and one image swap from a generic picture to a collage of real customer-content output up to 78 percent (a B2B agency client). claim: When buyers object to price versus competitors, moving trust elements above the price and risk badges under add-to-cart lifted conversion 30 to 88 percent in agency tests.
body: A price objection is often a risk objection: the buyer is unsure the higher price is worth it, so the page should answer that before the number appears and at the moment of commitment. In one ecommerce client test, the agency moved the price lower on the product page and placed trust-building elements above it; conversion rose 32 percent, and adding more trust elements ahead of the price took the cumulative lift to 88 percent. For another client (Parcel Safety) they added a row of badges directly under the add-to-cart button, covering free 30-day returns, a 100 percent money-back guarantee, a one-year warranty and free US shipping; the A/B test showed about a 30 percent conversion lift versus no badges. How to apply: list the doubts that stop a purchase (will it work, can I return it, how long to arrive, extra costs), put proof such as reviews and guarantees before the price, and put the specific risk-reversal terms in a compact row under the buy button. Sample sizes and test durations were not given, so treat the figures as directional.
conditions: Product pages where the product is priced above visible competitors and the store can actually honour the guarantee, return and warranty terms shown.
fails_when: Lowest-price products where cost is not the hesitation; when badges promise terms the business cannot afford or does not offer; cluttered pages where more badges push the buy button below the fold on mobile.

claim: End a personalisation quiz with a summary that plots the visitor's own numbers to a goal on a specific calendar date, before showing the buy box.
body: The strongest commitment device in the teardown is a results page built from the visitor's inputs. Mechanism: seeing their own current weight, target weight and a dated finish line makes the outcome feel real and close, so by the time the offer appears the visitor has argued themselves into it; the offer itself becomes secondary after a long quiz. How to apply: 1) Early in the quiz, ask for the goal picture (choose the body type you want) and current and target numbers. 2) Ask whether an important event is coming up (holiday, wedding) and its date; this ties the goal to a deadline. 3) Mid-quiz, show a chart from current to target with a projected date, for example 90 kg to 80 kg by a named date about three months out. 4) After the email capture, show a loading screen ('building your plan'), then a commitment pop-up ('will you start today?'). 5) On the summary, show 'now versus you in X months' with the image they picked; the practitioner prefers real dates over 'in 6 months' because far-off periods feel abstract. 6) Then reviews and the buy box with a visible discount timer and money-back guarantee, and remove any links that let people leave at that step. For a physical product, swap the app plan for a product carousel and UGC.

fails_when: Projected outcomes would be health or efficacy claims the brand cannot substantiate (regulated supplements, medical devices, ad-policy limits on weight-loss claims); or the product has no measurable personal outcome to project.

claim: In long quiz funnels, insert an informational 'micro-commitment' screen every 3 to 5 questions and vary input types to prevent answer fatigue.
body: The practitioner's rule, from quizzes his agency has run, is that a quiz which asks 20 or more button-click questions in a row loses people to answer fatigue. The fix is pacing. Mechanism: each info screen gives something back (a fact, a validation, an 'you are not alone' message), so the visitor feels they are getting value and keeps trusting the process, and a change of input type forces fresh attention. How to apply: 1) After every 3 to 5 questions, place a screen that reflects the last answers back, such as 'you drink more water than 50% of users' or 'nutrition drives most of your result', worded to match the goal they chose. 2) Swap copy on these screens by branch: a lose-weight answer and a gain-muscle answer should see different text. 3) Mix input types: numeric fields for height and weight, like or dislike or neutral ratings for activities, image choices for the body they want, multi-select for foods, not only single-choice buttons. 4) Include one setback question and answer it with a reassurance screen. 5) Use calming colours on reassurance screens. claim: Cutting a bundle picker from five pack options to three lifted conversion 53% and AOV 13.5% in one agency test on a drinks brand.
body: The agency tested a product page for Wildman Drinking (drinking accessories) that offered five bundle sizes. Session recordings showed visitors hovering between options and then leaving, a sign of choice overload at the most important decision on the page. The variant offered three options only: one pack, three pack and five pack. The reported result was a 53% increase in conversion rate and a 13.5% increase in average order value, meaning buyers both bought more often and picked larger packs. The mechanism is that every extra option adds a comparison the buyer has to make; with three clearly spaced options the choice becomes 'just one, a few, or a lot', and the middle option reads as the default. How to apply: look at your pack-size sales mix, keep the single unit, the pack you want most people to buy and one larger pack, and drop sizes that sell little and sit close to a neighbour. Then re-check AOV, not just conversion, because a lost in-between size can push some buyers down. The figures are agency-reported with no sample size or duration given.
conditions: Ecommerce product pages selling multi-packs or quantity bundles of one consumable or giftable product; mostly mobile paid traffic.
fails_when: Products bought in exact quantities for a known need (replacement parts, set-of-4 tyres, refills sized to a device); B2B or wholesale buyers who want fine quantity control; when the dropped size was a large share of revenue.
numbers: 5 bundle options to 3: +53% conversion rate, +13.5% AOV (agency-reported, Wildman Drinking, no sample size)

claim: Putting the dollar saving in each bundle's headline ('3 pack, save $10') instead of a small percentage underneath lifted conversion 25% and revenue per visitor 28.5%.
body: In the agency's test for Wildman Drinking, the original bundle selector listed a one pack, three pack and five pack with the saving shown as a percentage in small body text (save 10%, save 20%). Buyers had to notice it and do the arithmetic. The variant moved the saving into each option's headline as a dollar amount: 'three pack, save $10', 'five pack, save $20'. Reported results were a 25% higher conversion rate and 28.5% higher revenue per visitor; the presenter repeats the same test for a coffee brand in a companion video. The principle is 'don't make them do maths': the saving is the reason to choose a larger bundle, so it belongs where the eye lands first, written as money. This matches older direct-mail evidence that a dollar-off statement beats the equivalent percentage when the dollar figure is the larger number. How to apply: in the bundle or quantity-break selector, lead each option with the money saved versus buying singles, keep it consistent with the cart line and the ad, and verify the reference price is a price you really charge for singles.

fails_when: Low-priced items where the dollar saving is tiny (save $0.80) and a percentage reads bigger; reference price is not the real single-unit price, which breaks consumer pricing rules; agency-reported lift without sample size.

claim: A pre-lander advertorial that converts follows: call-out headline, credible narrator, symptom list, common enemy (why past fixes failed), mechanism and USPs, cost-of-inaction price anchor, offer, guarantee, two-option close.
body: The structure is built for mobile (the operator says nearly all readers are on phones) and for visitors who already saw a long-copy ad, so the page confirms rather than introduces. claim: A cold-traffic advertorial runs ten sections in a fixed order: hook, lived pain, failed alternatives, root cause, mechanism, proof story, objections, price and scarcity, guarantee, comments.

claim: Advertorials convert cold traffic at 3 to 4% versus 1 to 2% for product pages, but only when the ad starts the story and never shows the product.
body: The presenter, who runs advertorial funnels for brands, claims an article-style page converts cold traffic at roughly 3 to 4% where brands sending the same traffic to a product page see 1 to 2%, which lets them outbid competitors and hold ROAS at higher daily spend. No sample was given, so treat the gap as a practitioner estimate. The mechanism is that the page can only continue a story; it cannot start one. The ad's two jobs are to win the click and set the frame: it should look like a person sharing a discovery, not an ad, break an expectation (for example cancelling a planned surgery), open a loop (something a therapist said 'off the record'), qualify the reader in one line (age, condition), and tease the new cause without naming the product. Illustrated, comic-style or textbook-diagram images with no product shot worked best in his examples. The reader then lands mid-story on a page that looks like an article. How to apply: write the ad and the page's first screen together, reuse the ad's exact promise in the headline, and test the hook section hardest because nothing below it matters if it fails.

claim: List the five biggest buying objections, answer each with a testimonial from a different customer type, then reveal price against what the reader already spent on failed fixes.
body: Two late-page moves from the teardown. First, objection handling: instead of a generic review wall, pick the five objections that most often stop a purchase (will it work for my case, can I still do my hobby, is it safe, why did my doctor not mention it, how long is shipping) and place one testimonial against each, from a visibly different customer type so more readers find 'someone like me'. FAQ entries then close the remaining objections one by one. Use real reviews selected for this purpose; the presenter's advice to write testimonials and seed a comment section with scripted buyer chatter is fabrication and illegal in many markets. Second, price: the reader has no fixed sense of value, so the page sets the reference points before the number appears. The narrator has already spent over $5,000 on failed treatments, physical therapy cost $200 a session, and surgery would be $35,000 with a coin-flip success rate; against that, $59 feels trivial. Anchor against real alternative costs the buyer recognises rather than an invented 'suggested retail' price, which runs into reference-pricing rules.

claim: Name a root cause competitors ignore before revealing the product, and make every product component map one-to-one to that cause, or the page reads as a scam.
body: In the teardown, the page explains a cause before naming any solution: blood flow to the shoulder falls with age, so the joint is 'starving', not broken. The presenter's reasoning is that the brand that explains the problem best is believed to have the best solution before the solution appears, and if the reader accepts a new cause, every competitor is now solving the wrong problem. Only then is the mechanism revealed, and it must fit the cause exactly: heat opens vessels, compression pushes blood through tissue, vibration triggers repair, and the claim is that only the combination works, which shuts out cheaper partial substitutes like a heating pad alone. He says the page collapses if the mechanism does not map one-to-one to the stated cause. Credibility comes from specificity: each component gets a spec and a number. How to apply: write the root-cause paragraph first, check that each product feature answers part of it, and add a line on why partial solutions fail. Any physiological claim and any figure such as a percentage increase in blood flow must be substantiated; health and supplement claims are regulated, and an unsupported mechanism is a legal and ad-policy risk, not just a copy risk.

claim: An ad that barely sells needs a long advertorial lead (product hidden for 50 to 60% of the page); a long-copy ad needs a short lead.
body: Treat the ad and the landing page as two forces moving the same buyer from first contact to purchase. If the ad is a clickbait-style image built only to win cheap clicks, it has done no selling, so a product page will underperform; send that traffic to a long advertorial whose lead restates the problem, agitates it and intensifies desire before the product appears. In the speaker's example, the reader scrolls about 50 to 60% of the page before learning a product is being sold. If the ad already did the selling, such as a 1,000 to 3,000 word story ad, a 1 to 2 minute UGC video or a 4 to 5 minute video sales letter, a 3,000 word advertorial repeats what the visitor has just consumed. Use a short lead that shows the product in the first image or first few lines and gets to the offer fast. Style also depends on product type: improvement products (a better version of something known, such as antibacterial sheets) suit personal stories of failed alternatives; true novelty gadgets suit a 'breaking news' or revelation format that reaches the product quickly. How to apply: label each ad by how much selling it does, and pair it with a lander whose lead length is the inverse.

Promote: heavily clicked elements deserve size and position; image thumbnails shown as tiny dots still drew 7.35 percent of clicks, so they were made visible thumbnails, and the color selector drew 16.68 percent, so it was moved near the main image. claim: An advertorial must commit to one editorial identity for the whole piece (warning, discovery, whistleblower, comparison, local story); a sales letter with a news headline converts as neither.
body: The reviewer's top criticism of most advertorials is that they have no identity. An advertorial borrows its persuasive power from editorial content, so it must read as a recognisable kind of news piece from headline to close. A page that says warning in the headline but then runs a generic you have this problem, here is the cause, here is the fix structure is really a video sales letter in text, and loses the editorial credibility that makes cold readers keep going. He lists ten core types to choose from: breaking news or discovery; authority expert breaks down an issue; David versus Goliath; warning or fear; scandal or whistleblower; social proof (why everyone is talking about this); origin discovery story; comparison (I tested this against that); local or relatable person (an Ohio mom discovers); and scarcity or exclusivity (why this is about to sell out). If the angle is a hidden danger, the whole piece must be a warning promo; if it explains a new solution, the whole piece is a discovery promo. How to apply: before drafting, pick the type that fits the big idea and the target awareness level, then check that the headline, subheads and story all serve that type. claim: Open advertorials and ads with curiosity, proof and promise, not pain; everyone in a category shares the same pains, and AI copy defaults to leading with them.
body: The reviewer says leading with a list of pains (you cut out salt, you check labels, your face still swells) is the commonest weak opening, partly because AI copy tools default to it and readers now tune it out. Pains are shared by every product in a category, so they cannot make a reader stay; what is unique to your offer is your curiosity element (a new cause or mechanism), your proof and your specific promise. The strongest openings weave several copy blocks together in the first lines: if you have this pain, here is a simple curious thing that delivers this promise, backed by this proof, without these constraints. Pain still belongs in the copy, but only after permission is earned; going straight into someone's pain reads as presumptuous. Use softeners: maybe you tried dieting every day and it got harder, a first-person story (I don't know if you can relate, but I was...), or a third-person one (the patients I talk to feel...). Headlines should carry one main curiosity element, at most two, and stay universal rather than narrowing to details such as after your shift. How to apply: rewrite the first 50 words so curiosity and proof appear before any pain statement, and add maybe or a story frame to every direct pain line.

claim: Rank pain points for direct response by urgency, market size and direct product relevance; then use a familiar intermediary (e.g. detox) to reach bigger, more urgent pains.
body: Direct response asks for a purchase now, so it needs pains with high energy behind them: embarrassing, feared, or tied to big desires. The reviewer ranks a chlorophyll drop's pains by balancing three things: urgency, the scale of the market reachable, and how directly the product connects. Bloating and weight came first (huge market, direct link), then gut and digestion, then energy (a nice-to-have, harder to sell), then internal odour (urgent but small, so a secondary benefit or a niche funnel). Next he identifies an intermediary: a familiar concept on the way to the product's own mechanism, here detox. Asking which urgent problems people already associate with the intermediary opens new entry points (liver, blood sugar, inflammation, hormones) that can lead back to the product. He would spread testing like a portfolio, roughly 30% unaware angles from the broad pains, 30% problem-aware angles on the core pains, the rest on solution and product-aware. How to apply: score each pain 1 to 5 on urgency, scale and relevance, pick the top two as core angles, then list pains linked to your intermediary for unaware tests. Any health benefit you lead with must be backed by evidence for your product.

claim: Write advertorial copy at about a grade 5 reading level in full flowing sentences, with metaphors one step from the reader's mental picture (clogged filter, not factory).
body: Readers skim ads while doing something else and think concretely, so every extra mental step costs attention. The reviewer measured the submitted advertorial at grade 7 to 8 and wants grade 5 at most; an advertorial may sit slightly higher because it imitates editorial writing, but not much. Simplify by using short, earthy Germanic-rooted words instead of Latinate ones and plainer sentence structure, without making it shorter or less intense. Watch for two AI habits: staccato fragments (under your skin, around your belly, in your face) that break rhythm, and stiff academic phrasing. Prompt AI to use full grammatical sentences with natural conversational flow, then to lower the reading level to grade 3 to 5. Metaphors must match the rough sketch people already hold: most people picture the liver as a filter, so clogged or backed-up works instantly, while a factory adds a layer of abstraction and a mop does not match unclogging a filter. Avoid asking readers to do maths or imagine abstract timelines. Each fuzzy metaphor is a small paper cut that adds cognitive load. How to apply: run copy through a readability checker, list every metaphor and ask whether a distracted reader would picture it correctly in one second.

claim: In a pre-sale quiz, every question must win a micro-commitment, seed a buying belief, or pre-handle an objection; aim for about 8 to 12 questions, easiest first.
body: The speaker argues quizzes convert cold traffic not because of personalisation but because a run of small taps puts the buyer in a primed, agreeable state before the offer appears, and the ad CTA can be 'take the quiz' instead of 'shop now'. Design rules: each question needs one of three jobs. Micro-commitment: any tap or slider moves the visitor closer to a sale. Seeding: the question plants a belief the purchase depends on, for example a 1 to 10 slider on how much gut symptoms affect daily life reframes a nuisance as a quality-of-life problem. Pre-handling: 'how quickly do you expect results?' sets expectations before 'it takes too long' becomes an objection; 'what have you tried before?' meets 'nothing works'. Use in-quiz cards between questions to state the belief or proof. Order by gradualisation (Eugene Schwartz): open with a non-invasive goal question and leave personal items such as age, weight or symptoms for later. Vary format, never more than two or three of the same type in a row (multi-select, single choice, yes/no, slider), and make selections visibly respond. Avoid typed-answer questions: they feel like far more effort and cause heavy drop-off. Length: 3 to 20 works, 8 to 12 is his sweet spot. He says even a 3-question quiz in front of a sales page has almost always raised conversion for him, though he gives no test data.
conditions: Cold paid traffic; considered or problem-solving purchases, especially health, wellness, supplements and skincare; brands with research on buyer beliefs and objections.
fails_when: Simple impulse products where any step before the product page is friction; returning or warm traffic that already knows what it wants; health quizzes whose framing creates prohibited medical claims; long quizzes with no reason for each question.

claim: Print studies found reversed (light-on-dark) body text up to 16% less legible and all-caps headlines about 12% slower to read than initial caps.
body: Whitman collects classic readability research to argue that design choices cost readers. Reversed type: in a replication of a Starch experiment, a passage in white on black was 4% less legible when readers had just seen the normal version, and 16% less legible when shown on its own. All capitals: Paterson and Tinker (1956) found all-uppercase text slowed reading by 11.8%; a later challenge found an 18.9% gap in favour of initial-cap headlines. Typeface: Wheildon (1986) reported 67% comprehension for a serif passage against 12% for sans serif in print, and Paterson and Tinker (1932) found most faces read at similar speed except blackletter (16.5% slower) and typewriter-style (5.1% slower). Rules of thumb: set body copy dark on light, use sentence or initial case for headlines longer than a couple of words, keep about 70 to 80% one-syllable words and sentences near 11 words. How to apply: on product pages, emails and text-heavy statics, keep long body copy out of reversed blocks, avoid all-caps for anything longer than a short label, and save decorative fonts for logos. Treat the serif finding as print-only and contested.
conditions: Text-heavy surfaces: long product descriptions, advertorial pages, email bodies, static ads with several lines of copy.

claim: Test 20 to 40 headlines per Meta ad, then copy the winner into the landing page headline, subheadline and opening lines; reported lift: at least 15 to 20%.
body: An ad headline is seen by many times more people than ever reach the landing page, often around a thousand times as many, so Meta returns a readable answer on which message works far sooner than a page split test can. Use that cheaper test to choose the page's message, and keep the page in line with what people clicked. The speaker runs 20, 30 or 40 headlines per ad variant, picks the best on results, and puts the same words in the landing page headline, the subheadline and the first lines of copy. He reports this raises page conversion by at least 15 to 20%, and links many cases of cheap clicks but poor CPA to a mismatch between the ad and the page. He also keeps at least three split tests running at all times. How to apply: line up your top three ads' headlines next to their landing page headlines; fix any mismatch within a day; then test page variants built from the winning ad language, judged on conversion rate. The lift figure comes without a sample size, so treat it as a likely direction, not a promise.

claim: Send ads featuring a big ambassador to a dedicated landing page built from that person's shoot, so the page matches the ad; add a product carousel and the collab story.
body: Alo Yoga routes ads featuring one celebrity ambassador to a custom collab page filled with that shoot's images. It also notes other fashion brands doing well with it. They guess Alo has not built pages for other recent ambassadors because contracts limit how a celebrity's image can be used on site. claim: When paid traffic lands on a fashion collection grid, conversion depends on the top six products and their size stock; someone must check that grid daily.
body: About three quarters of Alo Yoga's paid traffic goes to category pages, mostly New Arrivals and Best Sellers. The agency's point for any fashion brand doing the same: a collection page converts or fails on what sits in the first six slots. If those are weak or unpopular items, the page underperforms; if they are winners, it converts. The hidden trap is size curves: the winning product may sell mostly in, say, black and blue in medium and large. When those variants sell out, the agency estimates a large share of traffic (perhaps 30%) hits out-of-stock options and conversion drops, even though the product still looks available. How to apply: 1) assign an owner (e-commerce manager or head of digital) to the paid-landing grids; 2) review the top rows daily against sell-through and variant stock; 3) push products with broken size runs down or out of the top six; 4) monitor conversion rate per landing page daily so a drop is caught within a day; 5) tighten white space so products appear above the fold. Outside fashion, a custom landing page is usually safer than a grid.
conditions: Apparel and footwear brands sending paid traffic to collection or category pages with fast-moving size runs.
fails_when: Non-fashion stores with few variants, where a custom landing page usually beats a grid; small catalogues with stable stock.

claim: Route traffic by awareness: unaware ads to third-party advertorials or quizzes, persona ads to matching persona pages, retargeting to product pages; IM8 sent ~150 of 700 ads to persona pages.
body: IM8 splits landing pages by persona and stage of awareness in three tiers. Top: advertorials and quiz funnels on separate domains, sometimes run from doctor or third-party pages, which educate unaware and problem-aware people before redirecting them to the store; IM8 retired its main quiz funnel in July 2026 after pointing a large share of ads at it, so this tier is not guaranteed to work. Bottom: product pages for retargeted, educated traffic. Strong trust layers on these pages (an ambassador wall, a science stack) are hard for competitors to copy, unlike generic trust badges. The speaker's critique: 88 ads pointed to the homepage, which tries to serve every persona at once; its conversion rate looks good only because organic traffic inflates it. How to apply: tag every ad by awareness stage and persona, check where each points, build a persona page whenever a new angle wins, and avoid sending cold paid traffic to the homepage.

claim: True Classic lost revenue when it added category breadcrumbs to product pages; links away from the product gave shoppers more ways to wander off and forget to buy.
body: Bartlett's example of a test he expected to win: adding breadcrumb links at the top of the product page so shoppers could jump to other categories quickly. It lost revenue. His explanation is that every exit route from the product page invites browsing, distraction and abandonment. He admits he would accept a small revenue loss for easier navigation if it improved the product mix in the cart, a judgement call rather than a rule. Related views from the interview: heat maps show almost nobody scrolls past the fold on the home page, so treat the home page like a concise landing page that hits the core value propositions (they lead with side-by-side fit comparisons rather than lifestyle images); and the most common testing mistake is changing too many things at once, so you cannot tell what caused the result. How to apply: test removing or demoting links that leave the product page (breadcrumbs, cross-category banners) while keeping links that add to the same purchase (pack builder, complementary items); change one thing per test. No numbers given for the loss.

fails_when: Large catalogues where shoppers need to compare across categories; SEO needs for breadcrumb navigation and markup (keep breadcrumb schema even if visually demoted).

claim: True Classic's cart gift ladder: free shipping at $100, a free shirt at $150, free joggers at $200; with multi-packs, its AOV rose from $36 to $112.
body: Co-founder Ryan Bartlett says the cart is where the most impactful conversion and order-value work happens. The structure is a tiered gift with purchase: reach $100 and shipping is free, $150 adds a free shirt, $200 adds free joggers. Two effects: shoppers add items to unlock the next gift, raising order value; and the gifts come from categories the buyer was not shopping (a t-shirt buyer receives an activewear shirt), so they try a new line and come back for it. Together with selling almost everything in packs rather than singles, with a pack builder on the site, he credits this approach with taking average order value from $36 to $112. How to apply: 1) set the first threshold a little above current AOV and later tiers at realistic stretch points; 2) choose gifts with low landed cost but high perceived value, from categories you want to seed; 3) show a progress bar in the cart; 4) check contribution margin per order at each tier, including gift cost and shipping. The $36 to $112 change spans years and several levers, so it is not the effect of the ladder alone.
conditions: Apparel or multi-category brands with repeatable basics and gifts that cost little to add to a shipment.
fails_when: Single-product stores with nothing to gift; thin margins where the gift cost erases the AOV gain; thresholds set so high almost nobody reaches them.

claim: Under India's E-Commerce Rules 2020, an online store or marketplace seller must show the total price with a breakdown of other charges, country of origin, importer details for imports, return and delivery terms, and grievance officer contacts.
body: The Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 cover marketplace entities, sellers on marketplaces, and inventory e-commerce entities, which sell stock they own; a brand selling its own products on its own website is the inventory model. IndiaLaw's summary lists what a seller on a marketplace must give the platform to display: legal name and address, website and customer care details, GSTIN and PAN where they apply, the total price with a breakdown of charges, mandatory notices and expiry dates, product details including country of origin, grievance officer contacts, importer details and guarantees for imported products, return and refund terms including shipping costs, and delivery details. An inventory entity must itself display returns, refunds, exchanges, warranties, delivery, shipping costs, payment methods, payment security, how to cancel and any fees, the total price broken down into charges such as delivery and taxes, and a ticket number for tracking complaints. Every e-commerce entity must show its legal name, head office and branch addresses, and customer support email and phone. How to apply: give every product a country of origin field and, for imports, the importer's name; show one all-in price with delivery and other fees itemised before payment; and link the return policy and grievance officer from every product page and the footer.
conditions: Online sales of goods or services to consumers in India, through an own website or a marketplace.
fails_when: From 1 January 2027 the 2026 amendment adds fields (full country of origin, GSTIN or MSME number); see that card. Food has its own labelling law. This is a law-firm summary, so check the rule text before a dispute.

claim: India's 2026 E-Commerce amendment, in force 1 January 2027, adds GSTIN or MSME number and full country of origin to listings, a copy of the recorded complaint for buyers, and the seller's name on invoices in the platform's font size.
body: SCC Online's summary of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026, notified on 9 September 2026 and effective 1 January 2027, lists these changes. Every e-commerce entity must prominently show its legal name, principal address, website, and customer care and grievance officer contacts. Grievance officers must acknowledge a complaint within 48 hours, give the complainant a copy of the complaint as recorded, and resolve it within one month. Entities selling imported goods must disclose the importer's details and the full country of origin. Invoices must show the seller's name in the same font size as the platform's name. Sellers must display country of origin, best before or use by dates where relevant, return, refund and exchange terms, warranties, delivery details, return shipping costs and payment methods, and under new Rule 6(5)(j) a government ID number such as GSTIN or MSME registration. Marketplaces must explain in plain language the main factors behind product rankings, may not use consumer data to promote their own brands or present sellers as linked to them without express consent, and may not charge bundled fees for services unrelated to the platform, except loyalty or membership programmes. How to apply: add GSTIN to listings and the store footer, store a complaint copy with each ticket, and check invoice templates before January 2027.
conditions: Sellers, D2C stores and marketplaces selling to consumers in India from 1 January 2027.
fails_when: The article does not say whether a standalone D2C site is treated differently from a marketplace seller, or how the dark pattern self-audit is filed. Check the gazette notification for exact wording.
